data.text:
F23 and F22 are fixed at records 103 and 105, and verified independently of the
implementer that wrote them. Three things this note records: how F23 was proved, two new
findings this round produced, and one mistake of mine.

## F23, proved by reverting it

A probe that only shows the delete refused proves nothing, because the delete is refused
today for a caller that can see the tenant row: `exists` is true, the branch is not
taken, and the raise happens for the ordinary reason. My first probe made exactly that
error and reported a refusal that the unfixed code would also have given. The
discriminating case is a role no policy on `public.tenants` covers, so the row exists and
is invisible, with a policy on `audit_events` that lets it reach the row at all.

Measured in rolled-back transactions, with the fix and then with the function replaced by
its pre-fix invoker-rights body:

| | tenants visible to the caller | audit row reachable | delete |
|---|---|---|---|
| security definer | 0 of 1 | 1 | refused 23001 |
| invoker rights | 0 of 1 | 1 | accepted, 1 row deleted |

The erasure cascade still takes a tenant's audit events with it, so the exception the
branch exists for is intact.

## F24, new, low: the restrict claim has the same defect F22 had

Part 5's header says a restricting key would mean the cascade from an erased tenant
reaches these children and "the whole erasure would roll back mid-statement", and its
self-check message says a restricting key refuses "a delete of the parent outright, which
is what a tenant's erasure is". The implementer found this while fixing F22 and I
confirmed it: with `claims_credited_by_settlement_line_id_fkey` as `on delete restrict`,
deleting the parent settlement line is refused 23503, and `delete from public.tenants` is
accepted. Same sibling-ordering reason, same shape of error.

The exclusion of restrict is still right, because it breaks the ordinary parent delete.
Only the stated reason is unreproducible. It is recorded rather than fixed because this
round was asked for F22 and F23, and F22 named the set-null sentence alone; widening a
round to the next sentence of the same kind is a decision for whoever owns it, not a
liberty a fix round takes.

## F25, new, low: an unreproduced failure and a registry that grows

One run of `pnpm --filter @seen/core test` reported 1 failed of 93 between green 105 and
this note. Four consecutive runs afterwards are green at 93, and I could not reproduce it.
I am recording it unexplained rather than explaining it, because a cause I cannot
demonstrate is worth less than an honest absence of one.

One plausible mechanism was checked and ruled out. `seen.erased_tenants` now holds 91 rows
and grows with every run, because the tests that seed and erase a tenant outside a
transaction leave their tombstones behind, which part 8 makes permanent by design. The
registry assertions are all scoped `where tenant_id = $1`, so none of them depends on the
table's size, and the growth does not explain the failure. The growth is still worth
closing: it is unbounded in every developer's local database.

## My own mistake, recorded because the receipt should not carry a claim I did not check

I committed 15075aa while that failing run was on screen. The command chained the commit
after a `grep` of the test output, so it ran on grep's exit status and not the suite's,
and the guard I thought I had was not there. The tree is green now and I have run it five
times since, so the commit's content is sound, but the verification I implied at commit
time had not happened. The fix is to make the suite's own exit status the gate, which is
what `harness check` does and what a hand-rolled pipeline does not.

F19 to F23 are now all fixed. F24 and F25 are open.
